hypothesis: If all living things share chemical composition, cellular structure and laws of growth and reproduction, then a large set of genes (the molecular machinery for those traits) must have recognisable orthologs across all three domains of life.
pass_criterion: Using OrthoDB's universal-level orthologous groups (root of life, with the Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryota subtrees), at least 30 orthologous groups, with functional annotation for translation, replication, transcription and membrane/energy metabolism, are present in at least 90% of sampled species of each of the three domains. In addition, at least 90% of the sampled eukaryote and prokaryote genomes carry orthologs of the core ribosomal-protein set. Thresholds were fixed before any data was seen.
fail_criterion: Fewer than 10 orthologous groups are present in at least 90% of species of every domain, or one of the three domains (Bacteria, Archaea or Eukaryota) shares fewer than 50% of the core ribosomal-protein orthologous groups with the other two. Either result would show that life lacks a common molecular core.
interpretation: Darwin's "chemical composition", "cellular structure" and "laws of growth and reproduction" are mapped onto shared molecular machinery, namely genes for protein synthesis, DNA replication, transcription, and cell-membrane and energy metabolism. Presence of orthologs across domains is the proxy for these shared features. This is a modern molecular reinterpretation. "Germinal vesicles" (the oocyte nucleus) has no direct genomic counterpart and is not tested. The poison-effect example is also not tested, because it is an illustration and not the generalisation itself. The test covers only the shared-machinery part of the claim; it does not measure chemistry or morphology directly. OrthoDB is a genome-based catalogue and does not record chemical composition, so shared chemistry is inferred from conserved biosynthetic and metabolic genes.

dataset.name: OrthoDB: the hierarchical catalog of orthologs (v13)
dataset.publisher: Zdobnov lab, University of Geneva / SIB Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics
dataset.why_it_fits: OrthoDB catalogues orthologous groups across about 5,800 eukaryotic, 18,000 prokaryotic and 8,000 viral genomes, at hierarchical taxonomic levels. Fields used: orthologous group ID, taxonomic level, number of species in the group, and the species-by-group presence table, from the data dump (odb_data_dump) or the API. These give the fraction of species per domain that carry each universal group. The ribosomal-protein groups can be identified through the functional annotation table.
